title: Smartphone alternatives for kids: 7 ways to stay connected without a full smartphone
summary: Compare 7 smartphone alternatives for kids, from home phones and flip phones to smartwatches, with pros, cons and questions to ask.
body_markdown:
Giving a child a way to communicate no longer means handing them a fully featured smartphone with unrestricted access to the world through the internet and apps. Families can choose from home phones designed for kids, basic flip phones, connected watches, GPS trackers, kids’ phones with built-in restrictions and, yes, smartphones with carefully limited features.


Parents searching for a smartphone alternative may be trying to solve very different problems. One parent may want to be able to call their child after school as they walk home. Another parent may want to call their child to let them know when they arrive for after-school pickup. Another might want their child to call before heading to a friend’s house. Some children may even just need maps, texting or location sharing so they can check in with their parents or find their way around.


Many parents face a practical dilemma: they want an easy way to reach their child, but they may not be ready to provide full smartphone access. In a[2025 Pew Research Center survey](https://www.pewresearch.org/internet/2025/10/08/how-parents-manage-screen-time-for-kids/) , 68% of parents of children aged 12 and younger said kids generally should be at least 12 before receiving their own smartphone. Lots of parents are worried that allowing their child to use a smartphone could open them up to inappropriate online content, hurt their development, give them too much screentime and lower their overall safety. Parents who do allow their children to use a smartphone, however, cited being able to contact their child as a major reason for allowing its use. Smartphone alternatives can help bridge that gap by providing specific communication tools without every feature of a traditional smartphone. It’s also important to remember, as the[American Academy of Pediatrics](https://www.aap.org/en/patient-care/media-and-children/center-of-excellence-on-social-media-and-youth-mental-health/qa-portal/qa-portal-library/qa-portal-library-questions/getting-your-first-phone/) notes, that getting a phone does not have to include getting social media.


School policies add another consideration. As of July 2026,[42 states, Washington, D.C., and Puerto Rico](https://www.ncsl.org/education/enacted-state-legislation-cellphone-use-in-schools) had enacted legislation related to cellphone use in schools. Many policies limit access during instructional time or throughout the school day. Some schools even confiscate devices for the day. Before buying a device, parents should understand what their child’s school permits and how the child can contact family when personal devices are unavailable.


The right choice depends on where a child needs to communicate, which functions they need and how much ongoing management the family wants to take on. Here is how the primary options compare.


## Smartphone alternatives at a glance


Option Mobile? Communication Internet or apps Location tracking Best fit


**Kids-focused home phone** No Voice calls No No Calling trusted people from home


**Basic or flip phone** Yes Calls and simple texts Varies Varies Simple mobile communication


**Kids smartwatch** Yes, with cellular service Calls and short messages Limited Usually Quick check-ins while away


**GPS tracker with calling** Yes, with service Limited calls or messages No Yes Location and caregiver contact


**Kids phone with built-in restrictions** Yes Calls and texts Curated or restricted Usually Mobile communication with controls


**Wi-Fi-only device** Only on Wi-Fi App-based calls and messages Yes, unless restricted Limited Communication from known locations


**Parent-managed smartphone** Yes Calls and texts Parent-controlled Yes Access to selected smartphone tools


Features vary by device and service plan. Parents should verify emergency calling, school rules, cellular compatibility and subscription requirements before buying.


## Before comparing devices, understand three types of protection


Products described as child-safe can take very different approaches to safety. Look closely at how each feature is handled:


- **Absent by design:** The device does not include the feature. A home phone without a browser or app store is one example.
- **Parent-restricted:** The feature is available, but a parent controls access through settings, approved contacts or app permissions.
- **Monitored:** The child can use the feature, while software reviews activity or alerts parents to potentially concerning content.


Each approach offers a different level of access and requires a different amount of parental involvement. Understanding the distinction makes it easier to compare claims such as “kid-safe,” “locked down” or “parent controlled.”


### 1. A kids-focused home phone


**Best for**


A home phone works well for children who need to call parents, relatives or approved friends from home. It can also help a child who arrives home before a parent, stays with a sitter or wants to speak with trusted friends or family independently.


**What it can do**


A kids-focused home phone provides calling without adding a browser, apps, games or social feeds. Ooma MyPhone, for example, lets parents create a Trusted Circle of approved contacts, limit outgoing calls to that list, schedule Quiet Hours and review call history. It also provides address-based 911 calling and can alert selected contacts when a 911 call is made. Parents must keep the registered location current for address-based 911 calling.


For families seeking a no social media option, these limits are built into the product and do not depend on app settings, saving the stress of having to continually monitor or manage app usage.


**What parents should consider**


A home phone stays in one location. Children cannot use it from school, activities or a friend’s house. Internet-based home phone service may also depend on power and internet access, so families should understand what happens during an outage.


**Questions to ask before buying**


- Can parents control incoming and outgoing contacts?
- How does 911 receive the home’s location?
- Does the service offer power or internet backup?


### 2. A basic or flip phone


**Best for**


A basic phone can suit children who need mobile calling and simple texting without the broad feature set of a smartphone. It may be enough for coordinating pickups or calling after an activity.


**What it can do**


Most basic phones provide cellular calls and SMS texting. Some include a camera, alarm, calendar, browser or simple apps. Physical buttons and relatively long battery life may also appeal to families.


Parents searching for a non-internet phone should check specifications carefully. There are now modern flip phones that are fully featured smartphones, and some of the more basic flip phones use simplified smartphone operating systems and still include Wi-Fi, a browser or app access.


**What parents should consider**


Many basic phones lack parent-managed contacts, location tools and remote controls. Children may be able to receive calls or messages from anyone. Group and picture messaging can also be limited, and older devices may no longer work on current cellular networks.


**Questions to ask before buying**


- Does it include a browser, Wi-Fi or downloadable apps?
- Can parents restrict contacts?
- Does it support the family’s carrier and messaging needs?


### 3. A kids smartwatch


**Best for**


A connected watch is useful for brief check-ins and location sharing while a child is away from home. Because it stays on the wrist, it may be harder to leave behind than a phone.


**What it can do**


Features can include calling, short messages, GPS location, approved contacts, geofencing, SOS functions and school-time settings. Some watches are designed for children, while certain mainstream cellular watches support family-managed setup.


Apple, for example, allows a parent with an iPhone to manage certain Apple Watch features for a family member who does not have an iPhone. Carrier support and available features vary.


**What parents should consider**


Small controls make watches better for quick exchanges than long conversations. Schools may treat connected watches like phones and restrict their use during the day.


Many smartwatches still have screens, notifications and interactive features. Their potential for distraction depends on the model and settings.


**Questions to ask before buying**


- Does it need a separate cellular plan?
- Can only approved contacts reach it?
- Will the school allow it?


### 4. A GPS tracker with voice calling


**Best for**


A GPS tracker fits families whose main priority is location awareness. It may work for a younger child who only needs limited contact with caregivers.


**What it can do**


Many trackers provide location updates, arrival alerts, safe zones and an SOS button. Some also support two-way calls, voice messages or preset responses. Most lack an open browser and app store.


**What parents should consider**


Location may update periodically rather than continuously. Accuracy can vary with cellular coverage, surroundings and battery level. A tracker shows where the device is, which may not always reflect where the child is.


Location history is sensitive data. Parents should review who can access it, how long the provider stores it and how the account is protected.


**Questions to ask before buying**


- How frequently does location refresh?
- Who receives an SOS alert?
- How is location history stored and protected?


### 5. A kids phone with built-in restrictions


**Best for**


A kids phone can provide mobile calling and texting while restricting browsers, app stores or social media. It can be a useful middle option for tweens and families seeking a safe phone for teens.


**What it can do**


Depending on the product and plan, features may include calling, texting, GPS, approved contacts, a camera, music, navigation and curated apps. Gabb Phone, for example, currently offers calling, messaging, GPS and preloaded or curated apps without an open browser, general app store or social media.


Some kids phones omit higher-risk features. Others provide access with parental controls or monitoring. The three approaches can create very different experiences even when products use similar safety language on websites and in ads.


**What parents should consider**


“Safe phone” is not a standardized category. Parents should compare the exact controls included with each plan. Some devices also require proprietary cellular service, specialized messaging apps or a long-term agreement.


Consider future flexibility as well. Check whether the phone number, contacts and photos can be moved to another service when the child’s needs change.


**Questions to ask before buying**


- Is the browser absent, filtered or hidden?
- Who controls contacts and app installation?
- Is proprietary service or a contract required?


### 6. A repurposed Wi-Fi-only phone or tablet


**Best for**


An old phone or tablet may be enough when a child only needs to communicate from home, a relative’s house or another place with trusted Wi-Fi.


**What it can do**


Messaging and video-calling apps can connect a child with family and friends without adding a cellular plan. Parents can remove unnecessary apps, block new downloads and use built-in parental controls.


**What parents should consider**


The device loses its communication functions when Wi-Fi is unavailable. Internet calling apps also handle emergency calls differently, so parents should verify whether 911 is supported.


A repurposed smartphone remains internet-capable even after apps are removed. It may require ongoing updates and account management. Older smartphone models may no longer receive critical security updates and may see lessened battery life.


**Questions to ask before buying**


- Where will the child have reliable Wi-Fi?
- Does the calling app support 911?
- Can downloads and account changes be blocked?


### 7. A standard smartphone with parental controls


**Best for**


A parent-managed smartphone may be appropriate when a child needs maps, school apps, transportation tools, team communication or accessibility features.


**What it can do**


Built-in controls can help parents approve apps, limit screen time, restrict content, schedule downtime and share location. Google Family Link supports app and screen-time management on supervised Android devices. Apple provides similar tools through Family Sharing and Screen Time.


Families can begin with calling, texting, maps and a few necessary tools, then add other features when needed.


**What parents should consider**


A smartphone requires the most ongoing management. Parents need to review permissions, approve apps, adjust limits and check settings after software updates. Filters and controls have limitations, and content can still arrive through approved communication tools.


**Questions to ask before buying**


- Which smartphone-specific functions does the child need?
- Can the browser and app store be restricted effectively?
- How often will the family review apps and permissions?


## How to narrow the options


Start with the situations in which your child needs to connect. A child calling trusted adults from home has different requirements from one coordinating rides across town. Compare the options based on:


- Where the device must work
- Whether the child needs calls, texts, location or specific apps
- Who can contact the child
- How emergency calling works
- What happens if power, Wi-Fi, cellular service or the battery fails
- How much setup and ongoing management the device requires
- The full cost of the device, service, accessories and replacements


## Finding the right smartphone alternative for your family


A home-based option such as MyPhone may be enough for a child who needs to call family and approved friends from home. A watch or tracker can support quick check-ins away from home. A basic phone provides straightforward mobile communication, while a kids phone with built-in restrictions adds texting and selected tools with more parental control. Children who need maps, school platforms or transportation apps may benefit from a carefully managed smartphone.


Each option combines connection, mobility and parental control differently. Matching those capabilities to your child’s daily life can help you avoid paying for features your family will not use or introducing access your child does not need yet.
